title: The Guru's Beard and Belly (മലയാളം)
summary: Guru Paramartha took extraordinary pride in two physical attributes: his magnificent, flowing silver beard, which reached down to his nav... [ML]
full_text:
Guru Paramartha took extraordinary pride in two physical attributes: his magnificent, flowing silver beard, which reached down to his navel, and his round, dignified belly, which he regarded as the sacred storehouse of Vedic wisdom. Every morning after his prayers, the Guru sat upon a wooden stool while his five disciples performed their assigned duties of grooming.

Matti was entrusted with combing the beard with a broad sandalwood comb; Madayan stood by with a clay bowl of perfumed sesame oil; Peedan held a polished bronze mirror; Asadan fanned away flies with a palm leaf, and Mudan sat cross-legged on the floor, holding the Guru's feet to ensure he did not tip over.

One morning, while Matti was combing the silver hairs with scholarly concentration, his hand twitched and the comb caught upon a stubborn snarl. Matti tugged with earnest devotion; a single silver hair pulled loose, and the Guru let out a sharp squeal of agony: 'Ai-yo! Matti, you clumsy fool, you have uprooted a root of wisdom from my chin!'

Terrified by his master's cry, Matti fell to his knees: 'Forgive me, Master! The hair was rebellious and refused to obey the sacred comb!'

Guru Paramartha stroked his chin with immense gravity: 'A rebellious hair must be reasoned with, not yanked. But look upon my noble belly! Is it not expanding with spiritual fullness?'

Madayan leaned forward and peered at the Guru's belly with profound scientific interest: 'Revered Master, your belly is indeed expanding like the crescent moon approaching fullness. But according to my calculations, if it expands another two inches, your center of spiritual gravity will shift, and you will tilt forward and tumble onto your nose!'

Alarmed by this philosophical prognosis, the Guru questioned: 'What is the remedy, Madayan?'

'The remedy is simple, Master!' proclaimed Madayan. 'To balance the heavy belly in front, we must tie an equal counterweight of stones to your back! Thus will perfect equilibrium be restored between front and rear!'

Delighted by this scientific logic, the Guru ordered five heavy granite grinding stones fetched from the kitchen. Matti and Peedan bound the stones securely to the Guru's shoulders and back with thick coir ropes.

'Now stand up, Master, and test your divine equilibrium!' cheered Asadan.

The Guru attempted to rise. But the combined weight of his majestic belly and the heavy granite stones proved too much for his knees. He wobbled, tipped sideways, and crashed onto the floor like a felled coconut tree, knocking Peedan into the oil bowl and sending the bronze mirror flying across the room!

As the Guru groaned beneath the pile of stones and his disciples scrambled to untie him, the village washerman who had come to collect laundry peeked through the gate, shook his head, and laughed: 'A belly full of rice needs fasting, not rocks, O wise master!'

Rubbing his bruised ribs, the Guru solemnly proclaimed: 'The washerman speaks from worldly ignorance; our equilibrium was merely disturbed by an unseasonable draft!'
moral: Fussing over outer appearances and bodily dignity blinds a man to his own absurdities. [ML]
